summary: State Bank of India helps households save, make payments and borrow, and lends to farmers, small businesses and large companies.
description: State Bank of India (SBI) runs bank accounts, branches, cash machines and a mobile banking app (YONO). A saver can receive income and pay bills; a farmer can borrow for a crop cycle; a business can finance stock or a larger project. SBI must assess those borrowers, collect repayments and meet its own payment obligations.
money: SBI earns interest on loans and investments and fees for relevant services. It pays interest on deposits and other borrowing, pays staff and technology costs, and makes provisions: charges or allowances for possible loan losses. Money deposited by a customer is owed back under the account terms, not earned as revenue.
customers: Households, farmers, small businesses, large companies and government-related customers use different accounts, loans and payment services. Borrowers pay interest; customers may pay service fees. Depositors can instead receive interest from SBI.
drivers: What funding costs, whether borrowers repay, the interest earned on loans and investments, service fees, running costs and the financial cushions available for losses and withdrawals.

groups.title: Household accounts, payments and loans
groups.examples: Savings and term deposits, home, vehicle, personal and education loans.
groups.explanation: A household may keep savings with SBI and borrow for a separate need. Deposits help fund the business but remain repayable; loans create interest income and the risk of missed repayments.

groups.title: Farm and small-business borrowing
groups.examples: Farm lending, Kisan Credit Card borrowing facilities and services for small enterprises.
groups.explanation: A farmer may need to pay for inputs before a harvest brings income. A shop may need stock before customers buy it. The bank lends against an expected ability to repay; seasonal and local business conditions matter.

groups.title: Larger companies and trade
groups.examples: Business and project loans, collections, trade and international payment services.
groups.explanation: A large project can need money long before it starts earning. The bank checks the repayment plan, any pledged security and how much it depends on that borrower or industry.

groups.title: Digital access and wider group services
groups.examples: YONO SBI, yono Business and relevant group financial businesses.
groups.explanation: Apps give access to banking and other offered services. Insurance, investment management and card businesses in the wider group have their own companies and costs; the app’s activity is not their combined profit.

basics.title: What does the bank earn from a repayment?
basics.text: The original loan amount is called principal. Paying it back returns money lent; interest is the additional amount charged for using it. That interest still has funding, operating and loan-loss costs to cover.

basics.title: Why does a bank need both capital and ready money?
basics.text: Capital is a cushion against losses. Liquidity means being able to make payments on time. Loans can take years to repay, so the bank must manage withdrawal needs and other bills alongside lending.

steps.title: Serve savers and arrange funding
steps.text: Provide accounts and payment access, pay applicable deposit interest and manage when funding must be repaid.

steps.title: Check each kind of borrower
steps.text: Consider a household’s income, a farmer’s crop cycle or a company’s business before agreeing the loan and repayment schedule.

steps.title: Collect interest and repayments
steps.text: Operate accounts, receive fees where applicable and monitor whether borrowers pay when due.

steps.title: Act on missed payments and maintain safeguards
steps.text: Follow up troubled loans, recognise potential losses and keep sufficient financial cushions and funds available for obligations.

specifics.title: Different loans fail for different reasons
specifics.text: A delayed harvest, job loss and unfinished industrial project affect different borrowers. Read the mix of lending and repayment performance instead of treating every loan as the same business.

specifics.title: A lower bad-loan balance needs an explanation
specifics.text: Problem loans can fall because of recoveries, a return to regular payments, sales or write-offs. A write-off changes the accounts and is different from receiving repayment. New problem loans can still be appearing.

specifics.title: A large network brings costs as well as reach
specifics.text: Branches, people and digital systems help serve customers but require spending and controls. More accounts or YONO registrations alone do not show that the service earns more after its costs.

watch: Can deposits support the pace of lending?
Loans need funding while customers still need access to money.
Compare lending, deposit types, deposit interest costs and other borrowing. Check the bank’s disclosed funds available for payment obligations, not only deposit growth.
Are fewer borrowers getting into difficulty?
A lower reported problem-loan balance can have several causes.
Read new problem loans, cash recovered, write-offs and provisions. Check repayment changes by available loan category and read any changed repayment arrangements.
What is changing interest earnings after funding costs?
Interest charged and paid can change on different schedules.
Read loan types, deposit pricing and investment income. If comparing net interest margin, check which assets, such as loans and investments, and which part of the bank the calculation uses.
Is the service network becoming efficient and reliable?
Reach must be supported by people, systems and safeguards.
Compare staff and other running costs with income and service activity. Read outages, fraud and technology disclosures alongside growth in accounts or app use.
Which results belong to SBI itself?
Controlled companies can add different financial businesses.

Use standalone accounts for the bank and consolidated accounts for the wider controlled group. Check capital cushions and available funds on the stated scope rather than mixing bank assets with group profit.
risks: Crop problems, job losses or weaker business demand can affect collections and increase losses.
Deposit interest costs can rise before the income from existing loans increases.
A large service network suffers failures
Cyber incidents, fraud, outages or rule breaches can affect many customers and cause losses.
More lending needs adequate capital and dependable funding as well as customer demand.
context: November 2026: loans still growing faster than deposits

SBI’s 3 November 2026 release for July–September 2026 reports loans up about 18 per cent and deposits up about 12 per cent compared with a year earlier, a smaller gap than in April–June. Most of the new deposits were fixed-term deposits, which cost the bank more interest than current and savings accounts. SBI’s exchange filings also record bonds raised in July and August 2026: money borrowed from investors that must be repaid with interest. Compare what each funding source costs with what new loans earn, and remember that a loan still has to be repaid over time before lending growth becomes a successful result.

July–September 2026 results press release · 3 November 2026 (NSE filing)

financialNotes.title: Verify the bank-specific financial measures
financialNotes.text: Use the consolidated annual column and its owners’ profit definition, including the adjustments for associates and minority shareholders. Interest earned, total income and net interest income are different measures. Deposit and loan balances are not product sales, and standalone-bank ratios should not be combined with group profit.

stepsTitle: From a deposit to a repaid loan.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: State Bank of India takes deposits from savers, handles their payments, and lends that money to households, farmers, small businesses and large companies.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Borrowers pay interest on their loans, and customers pay fees for some services. Savers are the other way round: SBI pays them interest on their deposits.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: Mostly from the gap between the interest it charges borrowers and the interest it pays savers, plus fees for services.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Interest on deposits, staff and technology, and provisions: money set aside in its accounts for loans that may not be repaid.

helps.title: A very wide range of customers
helps.text: SBI’s results split its loans between farmers, small businesses, households and large companies, and in July–September 2026 each group’s loans grew compared with a year earlier.

helps.title: A large network
helps.text: SBI’s FY 2025–26 annual report counts more than 23,000 branches and about 64,000 cash machines, and more than 60 per cent of new savings accounts were opened through YONO in April–June 2026. The network also costs money to run.

helps.title: Different loans, different risks
helps.text: A failed harvest, a lost job and an unfinished factory hit different borrowers, so lending to farmers, households, small firms and large companies spreads the risk. SBI’s annual report credits its diversified loan book for resilience. Its share of bad loans, those more than 90 days overdue, was lower in 2026 than a year earlier.

hurts.title: Borrowers face shocks
hurts.text: Crop problems, job losses or weaker business demand can slow repayments and increase losses.

hurts.title: Funding gets dearer
hurts.text: Current and savings accounts pay savers little interest; fixed-term deposits pay more. When more of SBI’s deposits are fixed-term, as in July–September 2026, it pays more for the money it lends, which can squeeze the gap it earns between loan and deposit rates.

hurts.title: Failures affect many customers
hurts.text: SBI’s annual report names cyber threats, disruptions and breaking rules as significant risks of its growing digital services, which serve a very large number of customers.

hurts.title: Growth needs more capital
hurts.text: Lending more needs enough capital, the bank’s own cushion against losses, and dependable funding.
